title: Stanford HAI Artificial Intelligence Glossary
source: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI)
content_note: Definitions are concise paraphrases of the Stanford HAI glossary, structured for machine-readable use.

terms.definition_summary: An attack that covertly interferes with a model-distillation or related training process to influence the resulting model.
A hypothetical AI system with broad, general-purpose abilities comparable to or beyond human capability across many tasks and domains.
AI designed to pursue goals with some autonomy by planning, using tools, making decisions, responding to feedback, and adapting its actions.
The effort to make an AI system’s goals and behavior consistent with human intentions, values, and rules.
Standardized evaluations used to measure and compare AI performance on defined tasks.
The ability to work effectively and responsibly with AI by understanding its strengths, limits, risks, and practical uses.
The field concerned with making AI systems reliable and reducing the risk that they cause harm.
The combination of software, hardware, infrastructure, and computing resources used to build, train, deploy, and operate AI systems.
The end-to-end process for creating and operating an AI system, including data preparation, training, evaluation, deployment, and maintenance.
A defined sequence of steps used to solve a problem or carry out a task.
A situation in which many organizations rely on the same or very similar algorithms, systems, or datasets.
A network of AI systems or agents that exchange information and coordinate their actions.
The science and engineering of creating machines or software capable of tasks associated with intelligent behavior.
A neural-network technique that lets a model emphasize the most relevant parts of its input while producing an output.
The use of technology to carry out tasks according to rules or instructions defined by people.
A learning method for neural networks that propagates prediction errors backward through the network to update model parameters.
Probabilistic graphical models that represent variables and their conditional relationships.
Systematic behavior in an AI system that can unfairly favor or disadvantage certain people or groups.
Very large or complex datasets that often require advanced computational methods to store, process, and analyze.
Software designed to interact conversationally with people through text, voice, or both.
Software whose source code is not publicly available for inspection, modification, or redistribution.
A field of AI focused on enabling computers to analyze and understand visual information such as images and video.
The amount of input information an AI model can consider at one time during a task.
A learning approach in which a model compares similar and dissimilar examples to learn useful representations.
A technique for expanding training data by creating modified versions of existing examples.
The process of finding useful patterns, relationships, or trends in large datasets.
An attack in which training data is deliberately altered, inserted, or mislabeled to influence a machine-learning model.
A model that makes predictions by repeatedly splitting data according to feature-based decision rules.
A branch of machine learning based on multi-layer neural networks that learn complex patterns from data.
Generative models that learn to create data by reversing a gradual noise-adding process.
A method for reducing the number of variables in data while preserving important structure or information.
Numerical vector representations that encode semantic or structural features of data such as text, images, or other objects.
Machine-learning techniques that combine predictions from multiple models to improve accuracy or robustness.
The design and use of AI in ways intended to support fairness, transparency, human values, and societal well-being.
An AI program that uses a knowledge base and rules to imitate expert decision-making in a specific domain.
Methods that make an AI system’s decisions or predictions easier for people to understand.
A training method in which a shared model learns across multiple devices or servers without centralizing their raw local data.
Learning or adapting to a new task using only a small number of examples.
Additional training of a pre-trained model on task-specific or domain-specific data.
A large, broadly trained model that can be adapted for many downstream applications.
A highly capable general-purpose AI model near the leading edge of current AI development.
AI systems that create new content such as text, images, audio, video, or code.
Generative architectures in which a generator and a discriminator are trained in competition to produce realistic synthetic data.
A family of transformer-based language models trained to generate and work with natural-language text.
A processor optimized for large numbers of parallel calculations, widely used for graphics and AI workloads.
A response produced by an AI system that is incorrect, misleading, or fabricated while being presented as if it were reliable.
An approach to AI development that prioritizes human needs, values, capabilities, and well-being.
The study and design of how people interact with computers and digital systems.
An AI setup in which people provide feedback, review, control, or intervention during operation or training.
A model configuration value chosen before or outside the main learning process rather than learned directly from the data.
A large technology provider operating massive cloud and data-center infrastructure that can scale computing resources quickly.
The stage where a trained model uses new input data to generate predictions, decisions, or outputs.
The degree to which people can understand how or why an AI system produced a particular result.
A machine-learning algorithm that predicts using the labels or values of the most similar nearby examples.
A structured representation of entities and the relationships that connect them.
A language model trained on very large text corpora to understand and generate human-like language.
A compressed mathematical representation in which complex data is encoded into underlying features or patterns.
Practices for deploying, monitoring, maintaining, and managing large-language-model applications in production.
A mathematical function that measures how far a model’s predictions are from desired or correct outcomes.
A branch of AI in which systems learn patterns from data to make predictions or decisions instead of relying only on explicit rules.
A probabilistic model where the next state depends on the current state rather than the full sequence of past states.
Engineering practices for reliably deploying, monitoring, updating, and maintaining machine-learning systems in production.
A mathematical or computational representation learned or designed to capture patterns and produce predictions or other outputs.
A decline in model performance over time as real-world data or relationships change from those seen during training.
AI systems that can work with more than one type of data, such as text, images, audio, or video.
A branch of AI concerned with enabling computers to process, understand, and generate human language.
A layered computational model made of interconnected units that learn patterns by adjusting numerical parameters.
A method for adjusting model parameters to reduce error or improve an objective during training.
A condition in which a model learns the training data too closely and performs poorly on new, unseen data.
An AI model released with enough underlying materials and permissions for others to inspect, run, modify, or reproduce it.
An AI model whose learned weights are publicly released for others to download and use.
Software whose source code is made available under terms that allow people to inspect, use, and often modify it.
An internal numerical value learned by a model during training.
The use of data, statistics, and machine-learning methods to estimate future outcomes or trends.
The practice of designing instructions and context to guide an AI model toward a desired response or behavior.
A security attack that uses crafted input to manipulate an AI model into ignoring or overriding intended instructions.
A technique in which a language model retrieves external information and uses it as context when generating an answer.
An AI system optimized for solving complex tasks through structured intermediate reasoning or problem-solving steps.
A machine-learning approach in which an agent learns through actions, feedback, rewards, and penalties.
Principles and practices aimed at developing and deploying AI in safe, ethical, accountable, and trustworthy ways.
The field of designing and building machines that sense, decide, and perform physical actions, often using AI.
The ability to understand three-dimensional space, object relationships, movement, and physical interaction.
A learning approach in which training targets are derived automatically from the data itself rather than supplied manually.
The analysis of language to determine meaning and relationships among words, phrases, and symbols.
Empirical relationships describing how model performance changes as factors such as model size, data, or compute increase.
Machine learning in which models are trained on examples paired with known target labels or outputs.
Artificially generated data created by algorithms or simulations rather than collected directly from real-world observations.
A multidimensional array of numbers used to represent and process data in machine-learning systems.
The process of splitting text into smaller units, called tokens, that a language model can process.
Earlier AI approaches based mainly on explicit rules, symbolic logic, and hand-crafted knowledge rather than data-driven learning.
The examples used to teach a machine-learning model how to perform a task.
Reusing knowledge from a model trained on one task as a starting point for another related task.
A neural-network architecture built around attention mechanisms for modeling relationships within input data.
A test proposed by Alan Turing to evaluate whether a machine’s conversational behavior can be indistinguishable from that of a human.
Machine learning that finds patterns or structure in data without labeled target answers.
A database optimized for storing and searching high-dimensional vector representations such as embeddings.
A transformer-based architecture adapted to process and analyze image data.
Learned numerical parameters that determine the strength of connections and influence a neural network’s computations.
The ability of a model to handle tasks or categories it was not explicitly trained on by using broader learned knowledge.
